cards.b: $Be > B$ and $N > O$ due to stable fully-filled/half-filled 2p configuration.
Net positive charge experienced by an electron after accounting for shielding by other electrons; $Z_{eff} = Z - \sigma$.

cards.f: Group with highest electron affinity magnitude (excluding noble gases)
cards.b: Halogens (group 17); Cl has highest electron gain enthalpy magnitude, more negative than F due to F's small size/electron repulsion.
Metallic character decreases across a period, increases down a group; opposite trend to non-metallic character.
Poor shielding by 4f electrons causes steady decrease in atomic size across lanthanoids, making 4d and 5d elements of same group nearly identical in size.
Valency = group number (for groups 1-14) or $8 -$ group number (for groups 15-18).
s-block (groups 1,2), p-block (13-18), d-block (3-12, transition), f-block (lanthanoids/actinoids).
$IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3 \ldots$; sharp jump occurs after removing all valence electrons (stable noble gas core).
He (smallest overall); among periods, radius decreases left to right, so noble gases/halogens of period are smallest (excluding van der Waals radius anomalies).
Atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve 8 electrons in the valence shell (noble gas configuration).

cards.f: Fajans' rules for covalent character in ionic bonds
cards.b: Covalent character favoured by: small cation, large anion, high charge on either ion, and cation with pseudo-noble gas configuration (18-electron).
2: linear; 3: trigonal planar; 4: tetrahedral; 5: trigonal bipyramidal; 6: octahedral (lone pairs distort further).

cards.f: Order of bond angles CH4, NH3, H2O
cards.b: CH$_4$ (109.5°) $>$ NH$_3$ (107°) $>$ H$_2$O (104.5°) — lone pair repulsion $>$ bond pair repulsion.
sp: linear (180°); sp$^2$: trigonal planar (120°); sp$^3$: tetrahedral (109.5°); sp$^3$d: trigonal bipyramidal; sp$^3$d$^2$: octahedral.

cards.f: Condition for a molecule to be polar
cards.b: Net dipole moment $\neq 0$; asymmetric shape or unequal bond dipoles that don't cancel (e.g. H$_2$O polar, CO$_2$ nonpolar).
$\text{Bond order} = \dfrac{N_b - N_a}{2}$ where $N_b$ = bonding electrons, $N_a$ = antibonding electrons.

cards.f: Bond order and magnetic nature of O2 (MOT)
cards.b: O$_2$: bond order = 2, paramagnetic (2 unpaired electrons in $\pi^*$ orbitals) — explained only by molecular orbital theory.
$\sigma$ bond: head-on orbital overlap along internuclear axis; $\pi$ bond: sideways overlap of parallel p-orbitals above/below axis.
Delocalization of electrons represented by multiple contributing structures; actual structure is a hybrid, more stable than any single structure.
$FC = (\text{valence electrons}) - (\text{lone pair electrons}) - \dfrac{1}{2}(\text{bonding electrons})$.

cards.f: Order of bond length for C-C, C=C, C≡C
cards.b: C-C (154 pm) $>$ C=C (134 pm) $>$ C$\equiv$C (120 pm); bond length decreases as bond order increases.
Intermolecular H-bond (e.g. between H$_2$O molecules, raises boiling point); intramolecular H-bond (e.g. o-nitrophenol, lowers boiling point/volatility).

cards.f: Dipole moment of NH3 vs NF3

$\Delta U = q + w$ (energy of universe is conserved); internal energy change = heat absorbed + work done on system.

cards.f: Work done in reversible isothermal expansion of ideal gas

$C_p - C_v = R$ (for one mole of ideal gas).

cards.f: Enthalpy definition and relation to internal energy
cards.b: $H = U + PV$; at constant P, $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$.

cards.f: Hess's law of constant heat summation

Enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states.

cards.f: Condition for exothermic and endothermic reactions
cards.b: Exothermic: $\Delta H < 0$ (heat released); endothermic: $\Delta H > 0$ (heat absorbed).

cards.b: At constant volume, $w = 0$, so $\Delta U = q_v$.
$\Delta S = \dfrac{\Delta H}{T}$ at the transition temperature (e.g. fusion, vaporization).

cards.b: State functions: $U, H, S, G$ (depend only on initial/final state); path functions: $q, w$ (depend on path).
Increases with higher ionic charge and smaller ionic radii (stronger electrostatic attraction).

cards.f: Free energy criterion with temperature (ΔH>0, ΔS>0)
cards.b: Non-spontaneous at low T, becomes spontaneous at high T when $T\Delta S > \Delta H$.
$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$.
No shift in equilibrium position; only speeds up attainment of equilibrium equally for forward and reverse reactions.
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that partially opposes the change.

cards.f: Effect of increasing temperature on exothermic equilibrium
cards.b: Shifts backward (endothermic direction), decreasing product yield.
$pH + pOH = 14$ at 25°C; $pH = -\log[H^+]$.

cards.f: Ostwald's dilution law for weak acid
cards.b: $[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a C}$; degree of dissociation $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$.

cards.f: Relation between pKa and pKb of conjugate pair
cards.b: $pK_a + pK_b = 14$ (at 25°C, in water).
$pH = pK_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$.
When $[\text{salt}] = [\text{acid}]$, i.e. $pH = pK_a$.

Addition of a common ion suppresses dissociation of a weak electrolyte / decreases solubility of a sparingly soluble salt.

cards.f: Nature of salt of weak acid + strong base
cards.b: Basic (e.g. CH$_3$COONa); hydrolysis produces OH$^-$.

Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base = electron-pair donor.
Fraction of total moles of a substance that dissociates into ions at equilibrium.

cards.f: Effect of inert gas addition at constant volume
cards.b: No effect on equilibrium (partial pressures/concentrations of reactants and products unchanged).

cards.f: Quick trick: reaction quotient Q vs K
cards.b: $Q < K$: forward shift; $Q > K$: backward shift; $Q = K$: at equilibrium.

cards.f: Oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons
cards.b: Oxidation = loss of electrons (increase in O.N.); reduction = gain of electrons (decrease in O.N.).

cards.f: Oxidation number rule for elements and monoatomic ions
cards.b: Element in free state = 0; monoatomic ion = charge on the ion.

cards.f: Oxidation number of O and H (general and exceptions)
cards.b: H = +1 (except metal hydrides: -1); O = -2 (except peroxides: -1, OF$_2$: +2, superoxides: -1/2).
Oxidizing agent: gets reduced, causes oxidation of another (gains electrons); reducing agent: gets oxidized (loses electrons).
Same element in one species is simultaneously oxidized and reduced, e.g. $Cl_2 + 2OH^- \to Cl^- + ClO^- + H_2O$.

cards.f: Balancing redox in acidic medium (ion-electron method)
cards.b: Balance atoms other than O, H → balance O with H$_2$O → balance H with H$^+$ → balance charge with electrons.

cards.f: Balancing redox in basic medium (extra step)
cards.b: Balance as in acidic medium, then add OH$^-$ equal to H$^+$ on both sides to neutralize, forming H$_2$O.

cards.f: n-factor of KMnO4 in acidic, neutral, basic medium
cards.b: Acidic: 5 (Mn$^{7+} \to$ Mn$^{2+}$); neutral/faintly alkaline: 3 (Mn$^{7+} \to$ Mn$^{4+}$); strongly alkaline: 1 (Mn$^{7+} \to$ Mn$^{6+}$).

cards.f: Highest and lowest oxidation states possible for an element
cards.b: Highest = group number (max electrons lost); lowest for p-block = group number $- 8$.
Two species of the same element in different oxidation states react to give a single intermediate oxidation state product.

cards.f: Rule for oxidation number of F in compounds
cards.b: Always -1 (most electronegative element, never positive).
Carboxylic acids $>$ anhydrides $>$ esters $>$ amides $>$ nitriles (then aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, amines, ethers).

$3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ >$ methyl (more alkyl groups = more hyperconjugation/+I stabilization).
Homolytic: bond breaks symmetrically giving two free radicals; heterolytic: bond breaks unevenly giving a cation and anion.

Carbocation (sp$^2$, planar, electron deficient), carbanion (sp$^3$, pyramidal, lone pair), free radical (unpaired electron).

cards.f: Order of acidity of carboxylic acid vs phenol vs alcohol

cards.f: Order of stability of alkenes (Zaitsev's rule)
cards.b: More substituted alkene is more stable/major product in elimination reactions (Zaitsev product).

cards.f: Markovnikov addition of water to alkyne (Kucherov's reaction)

cards.f: Coal and petroleum as hydrocarbon sources

Mixture of liquids with constant boiling point that distills without change in composition; minimum boiling (positive deviation, e.g. ethanol-water) or maximum boiling (negative deviation, e.g. HNO$_3$-water).

cards.b: $E^\circ_{cell} > 0$ (equivalently $\Delta G^\circ < 0$).

cards.f: Effect of dilution on molar conductivity
cards.b: Molar conductivity increases with dilution for both strong and weak electrolytes (increases sharply for weak, due to increased dissociation).
$m = ZQ = Zit$ (mass deposited proportional to charge passed).

Anode (oxidation, negative) written on left, cathode (reduction, positive) on right; e.g. $Zn|Zn^{2+}||Cu^{2+}|Cu$.

cards.b: Provides alternate pathway with lower $E_a$, increasing rate without being consumed; does not change $\Delta H$.

cards.b: $\text{mol}^{1-n}\,L^{n-1}\,s^{-1}$; helps identify order from given units.

cards.f: General electronic configuration of d-block elements
Why transition metals show variable oxidation states
cards.b: Both $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons have comparable energy and are available for bonding/ionization.

cards.f: Most common oxidation states of transition metals
cards.b: +2 and +3 are most common (Mn shows widest range, +2 to +7).

cards.f: Why transition metal ions/compounds are coloured
cards.b: d-d transition: unpaired d-electrons absorb visible light to jump to higher d-orbital (crystal field splitting), transmitted colour is complementary.

cards.f: Why Zn, Cd, Hg are not considered typical transition elements
cards.b: They have completely filled $d^{10}$ configuration in ground state and common oxidation states, so no unpaired d-electrons.

cards.f: Reason for catalytic activity of transition metals
cards.b: Variable oxidation states and ability to form intermediate complexes with reactants provide a lower activation energy pathway; large surface area also helps.

cards.f: Reason transition metals form complexes readily
cards.b: Small size, high charge density, and availability of empty d-orbitals to accept lone pairs from ligands.

cards.f: Common oxidation state and colour of KMnO4 and K2Cr2O7
cards.b: KMnO$_4$: Mn +7, purple; K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$: Cr +6, orange; both strong oxidizing agents.

cards.f: Highest oxidation state in d-block and where it occurs
cards.b: +8, shown by Os and Ru (in OsO$_4$, RuO$_4$) — matches group number.

cards.f: Lanthanoid contraction: general oxidation state of lanthanoids
cards.b: +3 is most common and stable; some show +2 or +4 due to extra stability of $f^0, f^7, f^{14}$ configurations (e.g. Ce$^{4+}$, Eu$^{2+}$).

cards.f: Why Cu(I) is unstable in aqueous solution but Cu(II) is stable
cards.b: Cu$^{2+}$ has higher hydration enthalpy that compensates for higher ionization enthalpy; Cu$^+$ disproportionates: $2Cu^+ \to Cu^{2+} + Cu$.

cards.f: Alloy formation tendency of transition metals
cards.b: Similar atomic size allows one metal to be replaced by another in crystal lattice, forming alloys (e.g. steel, brass, bronze).

cards.f: Trend in metallic/atomic radii across a transition series
cards.b: Decreases initially, becomes roughly constant in the middle, slight increase towards end due to increasing electron-electron repulsion in d-orbitals.

cards.f: E° value trend and stability: Mn3+/Mn2+
cards.b: High positive E° value shows Mn$^{2+}$ (half-filled $d^5$) is extra stable, making Mn$^{3+}$ a strong oxidizer.
Primary valency = ionizable, satisfied by anions (= oxidation state); secondary valency = non-ionizable, fixed (= coordination number), fixed geometry.
Number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal atom/ion.
-NO$_2$/-ONO (nitro/nitrito), -SCN/-NCS (thiocyanato/isothiocyanato) — bind through either of two donor atoms.
Ring formed when a polydentate ligand binds metal at 2+ points; increases complex stability (chelate effect), e.g. en, EDTA$^{4-}$.

cards.f: IUPAC naming order for coordination compounds
cards.b: Cation named first, ligands named alphabetically before metal, anionic complex ends in '-ate', oxidation state in Roman numerals in brackets.
$d^2sp^3$ (inner orbital, low spin) or $sp^3d^2$ (outer orbital, high spin) → octahedral geometry.
$sp^3$ → tetrahedral (e.g. [NiCl$_4$]$^{2-}$); $dsp^2$ → square planar (e.g. [Ni(CN)$_4$]$^{2-}$).

cards.f: Crystal field splitting in octahedral field
cards.b: d-orbitals split into $t_{2g}$ (lower, 3 orbitals) and $e_g$ (higher, 2 orbitals); splitting energy $\Delta_o$.

cards.f: Crystal field splitting in tetrahedral field
cards.b: Splits into $e$ (lower) and $t_2$ (higher); $\Delta_t \approx \dfrac{4}{9}\Delta_o$, always high spin.

cards.f: Strong field vs weak field ligands (spectrochemical series ends)
cards.b: Weak field: $I^- < Br^- < Cl^- < F^- < H_2O < NH_3$; strong field: $\ldots < CN^- < CO$ (cause pairing, low spin).
Isomers differ in the point of attachment of an ambidentate ligand to the metal (e.g. M-NO$_2$ vs M-ONO).
Isomers give different ions in solution due to exchange of ligand and counter ion, e.g. [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Br]SO$_4$ vs [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$SO$_4$]Br.

cards.f: Optical isomerism in coordination compounds occurs when
cards.b: Complex is chiral (non-superimposable mirror images), common in octahedral complexes with bidentate ligands (e.g. [Co(en)$_3$]$^{3+}$).
EAN = atomic number of metal $-$ oxidation state $+$ 2 $\times$ (number of ligand donor atoms); stable complexes often have EAN equal to next noble gas.
Homoleptic: metal bonded to only one kind of ligand (e.g. [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]$^{3+}$); heteroleptic: more than one kind (e.g. [Co(NH$_3$)$_4$Cl$_2$]$^+$).

cards.f: Why [Ni(CN)4]2- is diamagnetic but [NiCl4]2- is paramagnetic
cards.b: CN$^-$ is a strong field ligand causing pairing (dsp$^2$, square planar, diamagnetic); Cl$^-$ is weak field, no pairing (sp$^3$, tetrahedral, paramagnetic).
Used in treatment of heavy metal poisoning and estimation of water hardness (forms stable chelate with Ca$^{2+}$, Mg$^{2+}$, Pb$^{2+}$).

cards.f: Stability of complex and formation constant
cards.b: Higher formation constant $K_f$ ⟹ more stable complex; larger overall stability constant favours chelates over similar monodentate ligand complexes.
SN1: two-step, carbocation intermediate, favoured by 3° halides, racemization; SN2: one-step, backside attack, inversion (Walden inversion), favoured by 1° halides.

cards.f: Order of reactivity of alkyl halides towards SN2
cards.b: $CH_3X > 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$ (steric hindrance decreases rate).

cards.f: Order of reactivity of alkyl halides towards SN1
cards.b: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$ (carbocation stability determines rate).

cards.f: Reactivity order of C-X bond: alkyl vs aryl vs vinyl halide
cards.b: Alkyl halide $>$ vinyl/aryl halide (C-X bond in aryl/vinyl halide has partial double bond character due to resonance, harder to break).

cards.f: Why haloarenes are less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophilic substitution
cards.b: Resonance gives C-X partial double bond character (stronger, shorter bond); sp$^2$ carbon more electronegative; possible repulsion of nucleophile by ring electrons.
Aryl halide + alkyl halide + Na in dry ether → alkylbenzene (used to prepare alkylbenzenes with unequal alkyl groups).
$R-Cl/Br + NaI \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} R-I + NaCl/NaBr$; used to prepare alkyl iodides.
$R-X + AgF/Hg_2F_2/SbF_3 \to R-F$; used to prepare alkyl fluorides.

cards.f: Grignard reagent formation and general reactivity
cards.b: $RX + Mg \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} RMgX$; highly reactive, reacts with any source of active hydrogen (water, alcohol, amine).
Planar carbocation intermediate is attacked from both faces, giving a racemic mixture (partial or complete loss of optical activity).
$CN^-$: attacks through C (forms nitrile, R-CN) predominantly since it is more nucleophilic than N in $CN^-$; via N gives isocyanide (R-NC).
Bulky base and 3° substrate favour elimination (Zaitsev product, more substituted alkene); high temperature favours elimination over substitution.
Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane; effective insecticide but non-biodegradable, causes bioaccumulation — banned in many countries.

cards.f: Optical activity and chirality in haloalkanes
cards.b: A carbon with four different groups attached is chiral (asymmetric carbon), leading to optical isomerism (enantiomers).

cards.f: Preparation of haloalkanes from alcohols using PCl5/SOCl2
cards.b: SOCl$_2$ preferred (Darzen's process): by-products (SO$_2$, HCl) are gases, giving pure alkyl chloride easily.

cards.f: Why aryl halides undergo electrophilic substitution more readily than nucleophilic
cards.b: Halogen is o,p-directing but deactivating due to resonance donation of lone pair into ring, activating ring towards further electrophilic attack at o/p positions.
ROH + conc. HCl/ZnCl$_2$: 3° alcohol turns turbid immediately, 2° in a few minutes, 1° does not react at room temperature — distinguishes alcohol classes.

cards.f: Order of boiling points: alcohol vs alkane of similar mass
cards.b: Alcohols have much higher boiling points due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding, unlike non-polar alkanes.

cards.f: Acidity order: alcohol vs phenol vs water
cards.b: Phenol $>$ water $>$ alcohol (phenoxide ion stabilized by resonance; alkyl group's $+I$ effect destabilizes alkoxide).

cards.f: Effect of electron-withdrawing group on phenol acidity
cards.b: Increases acidity (e.g. p-nitrophenol $>$ phenol) by stabilizing phenoxide ion via resonance/induction.
Sodium phenoxide + CO$_2$ (heat, pressure) then acidify → salicylic acid (ortho-hydroxybenzoic acid).
Phenol + CHCl$_3$ + NaOH → salicylaldehyde (ortho-hydroxybenzaldehyde) via dichlorocarbene intermediate.
$R-X + R'ONa \to R-O-R' + NaX$; SN2 mechanism, best with 1° alkyl halide (3° halide gives elimination).
Excess HI cleaves ether to give alkyl iodide + alcohol/phenol; with 3° alkyl group, SN1 mechanism gives 3° iodide preferentially.

cards.f: Dehydration of alcohols: order of ease
cards.b: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$ (E1 mechanism via carbocation stability); follows Zaitsev's rule for major product.

cards.f: Test to distinguish phenol from alcohol
cards.b: Phenol gives violet/purple colour with neutral FeCl$_3$; alcohols do not.

cards.f: Preparation of alcohols from Grignard reagent
cards.b: HCHO gives 1° alcohol; other aldehydes give 2° alcohol; ketones give 3° alcohol (after hydrolysis).

cards.f: Why phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution readily
cards.b: -OH group is strongly activating (o,p-director) via resonance donation of lone pair into the ring, increasing electron density at o/p positions.
Lone pair on oxygen allows ethers to form oxonium salts with strong acids (e.g. with HI, H$_2$SO$_4$) and complexes with Grignard reagents/BF$_3$.

cards.f: Victor Meyer's test for distinguishing 1°, 2°, 3° alcohols
cards.b: Alcohol → alkyl iodide → nitroalkane → treated with HNO$_2$ then KOH: 1° gives red colour, 2° gives blue, 3° gives no colour.
Made by Williamson synthesis (phenoxide + CH$_3$I); -OCH$_3$ is o,p-directing and activating on the benzene ring.

cards.f: Nucleophilic addition reactivity: aldehyde vs ketone
cards.b: Aldehydes more reactive than ketones due to less steric hindrance and less +I effect (only one alkyl group vs two).
Aldehyde + Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO$_3$) → silver mirror; aldehydes give positive test, ketones do not.
Aldehyde (aliphatic) + Fehling's solution (Cu$^{2+}$ complex) → brick-red precipitate of Cu$_2$O; aromatic aldehydes do not respond.
Compounds with CH$_3$CO- group or CH$_3$CH(OH)- group give yellow iodoform (CHI$_3$) precipitate with I$_2$/NaOH.
Carbonyl compound with $\alpha$-hydrogen, dilute base/acid catalyst, gives $\beta$-hydroxy aldehyde/ketone, which on heating loses water to form $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated carbonyl.
Aldehyde with NO $\alpha$-hydrogen + conc. NaOH → disproportionation to one alcohol + one carboxylate salt (self redox).
C=O reduced to CH$_2$ using Zn-Hg/conc. HCl; used for acid-stable substrates.
C=O reduced to CH$_2$ using NH$_2$NH$_2$/KOH (or NaOH), heat; used for base-stable, acid-sensitive substrates.
Carboxylic acid with $\alpha$-H + X$_2$/red P → $\alpha$-halo carboxylic acid.

cards.f: Order of acidity of carboxylic acids with EWG/EDG substituents
cards.b: Electron-withdrawing groups (Cl, NO$_2$) increase acidity (stabilize carboxylate); electron-donating groups (alkyl) decrease acidity.
Acid chloride + H$_2$/Pd-BaSO$_4$ (poisoned catalyst) → aldehyde (prevents over-reduction to alcohol).

cards.f: Order of boiling points: carboxylic acid vs alcohol of similar mass
cards.b: Carboxylic acid $>$ alcohol; acids form stronger dimers via two intermolecular hydrogen bonds.
Nucleophile attacks electrophilic carbonyl carbon → tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate → protonation gives product.

cards.f: Test to distinguish aldehyde from ketone
cards.b: Tollens' or Fehling's test: aldehydes give positive result (silver mirror/brick-red ppt), ketones give negative result.
Sodium salt of carboxylic acid + soda lime (NaOH+CaO), heat → alkane with loss of CO$_2$ (one carbon less).
Toluene + CrO$_2$Cl$_2$ (chromyl chloride) then hydrolysis → benzaldehyde (direct oxidation of methyl group).

cards.f: Relative strength: formic acid vs acetic acid
cards.b: Formic acid (HCOOH) is stronger than acetic acid (no +I alkyl group to destabilize the carboxylate).

cards.f: Basicity order of amines in aqueous phase
cards.b: $2^\circ > 1^\circ > 3^\circ > NH_3$ (aliphatic); depends on +I effect, steric hindrance, and solvation of resulting cation.

cards.f: Basicity of aromatic vs aliphatic amines
cards.b: Aliphatic amines $>$ NH$_3$ $>$ aromatic amines (aniline); lone pair on N in aniline delocalizes into ring, less available for protonation.
Amine + benzenesulfonyl chloride: 1° gives soluble product (turns insoluble on acidification), 2° gives insoluble product, 3° does not react — distinguishes amine classes.
1° amine + CHCl$_3$ + alcoholic KOH → foul-smelling isocyanide (carbylamine); 2° and 3° amines do not respond — test specific to 1° amines.
Aromatic 1° amine + NaNO$_2$/HCl at 0-5°C → arenediazonium salt ($ArN_2^+Cl^-$).
$ArN_2^+ + CuCl/CuBr/KCN \to ArCl/ArBr/ArCN$; used to introduce Cl, Br, CN onto benzene ring via diazonium salt.
Diazonium salt + phenol/aromatic amine (in cold, alkaline/mildly acidic medium) → azo compound (coloured, used as dyes).
Used to prepare pure 1° amines only; avoids over-alkylation, since phthalimide N has no further reactive H after alkylation.
Amide + Br$_2$/NaOH → 1° amine with one carbon less (via isocyanate intermediate); used to step down in carbon chain.

cards.f: Effect of substituents on aniline basicity
cards.b: Electron-donating groups (o,p to NH$_2$) increase basicity; electron-withdrawing groups (especially at p-position, e.g. NO$_2$) sharply decrease basicity.

cards.f: Why aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction
cards.b: NH$_2$ group forms a salt with AlCl$_3$ (Lewis acid), becoming deactivating $-NR_3^+$ group, blocking the reaction.

cards.f: Reduction methods to prepare amines from nitro compounds
cards.b: Nitrobenzene + Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl or H$_2$/catalyst → aniline (reduction of NO$_2$ to NH$_2$).
3° amine + R-X → quaternary ammonium salt $R_4N^+X^-$ (no lone pair left on N, not basic, permanently charged).

cards.f: Diazonium salt as synthetic intermediate for phenol/nitrile/aryl halide
cards.b: Hydrolysis (H$_2$O/H$^+$, warm) → phenol; Sandmeyer with CuCN → nitrile; with CuCl/CuBr → aryl halide; makes ring substitution possible where direct methods fail.
Monosaccharides (cannot hydrolyse further, e.g. glucose); oligosaccharides (2-10 units, e.g. sucrose); polysaccharides (many units, e.g. starch, cellulose).
Reducing sugars have free -CHO/-C=O group, reduce Tollens'/Fehling's (e.g. glucose, maltose); non-reducing (e.g. sucrose) do not, as both anomeric OH's are involved in glycosidic bond.
$\alpha$-1,2 glycosidic linkage between C1 of $\alpha$-glucose and C2 of $\beta$-fructose; no free anomeric OH, hence non-reducing.
Amylose: unbranched, $\alpha$-1,4 glycosidic links, water-soluble; amylopectin: branched, $\alpha$-1,4 with $\alpha$-1,6 branch points, water-insoluble.
$\beta$-1,4 glycosidic linkage between glucose units; gives linear, fibrous structure (not digestible by humans, lacking cellulase).
Amide linkage (-CO-NH-) formed between -COOH of one amino acid and -NH$_2$ of another, with loss of water.
Essential: cannot be synthesized by body, must come from diet (e.g. valine, leucine); non-essential: body can synthesize (e.g. glycine, alanine).
Amino acid exists as dipolar ion $H_3N^+-CHR-COO^-$; at isoelectric point, net charge is zero and solubility/mobility is minimum.
Primary: amino acid sequence; secondary: $\alpha$-helix/$\beta$-pleated sheet (H-bonding); tertiary: 3D folding; quaternary: assembly of multiple subunits.
Loss of secondary/tertiary structure (biological activity) due to heat, pH change, etc., while primary structure (peptide bonds) remains intact.
Adenine pairs with thymine (2 H-bonds); guanine pairs with cytosine (3 H-bonds) — Chargaff's rule.

cards.f: DNA vs RNA: sugar and bases
cards.b: DNA: deoxyribose sugar, bases A,T,G,C, double-stranded; RNA: ribose sugar, bases A,U,G,C (uracil replaces thymine), usually single-stranded.

cards.f: Vitamin deficiency diseases: A, C, D
cards.b: Vitamin A deficiency → night blindness; Vitamin C → scurvy; Vitamin D → rickets (children)/osteomalacia (adults).
Water-soluble: B-complex, C (not stored, need regular intake); fat-soluble: A, D, E, K (stored in liver/adipose tissue).
Globular proteins that catalyze specific biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy; highly specific to substrate (lock-and-key model).
Chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands into blood, regulate body functions, e.g. insulin (regulates blood glucose).
Glucose cyclic forms ($\alpha$ and $\beta$) that differ only in configuration at the anomeric carbon (C1, the new stereocentre formed on cyclization).
